{"id": "5d4d0e19-6dbe-45f9-b349-418b24550bfb", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "`df -h` only shows block usage on the filesystem that holds `/`. "No space left on device" can also come from other limits, and your df output wouldn't show them. I haven't looked at the instance yet, so the causes below are ranked by how often they cause this exact dpkg error on Ubuntu. They aren't confirmed.

## Most likely causes

1. **Inode exhaustion.** This is the classic cause. The disk has free blocks but no free inodes, so dpkg can't create new files.
   - Check with `df -i /` and `df -i /var /boot /tmp`. If IUse% is at or near 100%, this is the cause.
   - Common culprits are millions of small files under `/var/lib/php/sessions`, `/var/spool`, `/tmp`, `/var/lib/docker`, or old `/usr/src/linux-headers-*` directories.
   - Find them with `sudo find / -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f1-4 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`.

2. **A separate, full mount.** dpkg writes to more than `/`.
   - `/boot` is the usual one on Ubuntu 22.04. Old kernels and initrd images pile up, and if `/boot` is a separate small partition, kernel package installs fail.
   - `/var`, `/tmp` or `/usr` can also be separate mounts.
   - Run `df -h` and `df -i` with no path, and look at every mount, not just `/`.
   - If it's `/boot`, run `sudo apt-get autoremove --purge` and remove old kernels.

3. **Deleted files still held open.** A process may be holding a large deleted file, such as a rotated log. The space isn't freed, though `du` and `df` can disagree.
   - Check with `sudo lsof +L1 | head`. Restart the offending service to release the space.

4. **Mount or filesystem oddities.**
   - Check whether `/var/cache/apt` or `/var/lib/dpkg` sits on a tmpfs or other small mount. `findmnt -T /var/lib/dpkg` and `findmnt -T /var/cache/apt` will show this.
   - Check for a read-only remount after I/O errors. `dmesg | tail` and `mount | grep ' / '` will show it.
   - Check for a bind mount that hides data on the underlying filesystem.

## Quick triage on the instance
```
df -h; df -i
findmnt -T /var/lib/dpkg
findmnt -T /boot
sudo lsof +L1 | head
sudo dmesg | tail -20
```

## After you free space
```
sudo dpkg --configure -a
sudo apt-get -f install
sudo apt-get autoremove --purge
```
dpkg may be left half-configured after the failure, so run these before you retry the patch.

If the root volume is genuinely too small, you can grow the EBS volume and then run `growpart` and `resize2fs`. That doesn't help if the problem is inodes on ext4, because you can't add inodes without recreating the filesystem. In that case, clean up the small files instead.

I can check the instance's EBS volumes and any CloudWatch disk or inode metrics from the AWS side. To do that, tell me the AWS account ID and whether the CloudWatch agent is installed. If you paste the output of `df -h`, `df -i` and `findmnt`, I can pinpoint the cause.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
